Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
733 AM EDT Sat Aug 29 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 221 AM EDT Saturday...

No significant changes were made to the forecast.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 221 AM EDT Saturday...

1. High pressure will dominate the region today through early 
Sunday. Rain chances, mainly north, return during the day Sunday as 
a cold front sinks south from Canada.

2. A period of shower weather is expected mid to late week, 
with a emphasis on Wednesday night into Thursday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 221 AM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure will continue to build in this morning 
with areas of patchy valley fog scouring out an hour or two after 
sunrise. Mainly clear skies aside from some fair weather cumulus in 
the higher terrain will create a pleasant day across the region. 
Some light breezes from southwest channeled flow in the St. Lawrence 
Valley to 10-20 mph will be possible, in addition to light southerly 
flow in the Champlain Valley to 15 MPH as well. Highs will be 
relatively seasonable in the mid 70s. High pressure will begin to 
dip south late this evening as a cold front from Quebec sinks south. 
A modest low-level jet to 40-50 knots will precede the frontal 
leading to gusty winds on mountain summits. Elevations above 2500ft 
agl could see southwest winds around 30 MPH, with very isolated 
gusts to near 40 MPH in the highest summits of the Adirondacks. Due 
to less friction, Lake Champlain may also see 10-20 MPH winds 
overnight. An inversion should help keep winds in the wider valleys 
and sheltered hollows generally under 10 MPH. 

Zonal flow ahead of a positively tilted shortwave, in association 
with the cold front, will keep moisture fairly progressive, but some 
shower activity will be possible near the International Border by 
mid to late Sunday. Lifting along the front with cool temperatures 
aloft may lead to some weak instability on the southern periphery of 
the front in northern Vermont and near the US-11 corridor in 
northern New York. The southern extent of the shower activity will 
be tricky with 10-20 degree dewpoint depressions Sunday afternoon as 
high pressure retreats south. Best shower chances will be closer to 
the International Border during the day. Rain amounts will generally 
be low from a few hundreths to a tenth or two in the western upslope 
areas. The front will slowly sag south Sunday night into north 
central Vermont and the northern Adirondacks. With fairly uniform 
flow under a zonal pattern, showers will become more confined to the 
western upslope regions of the Greens and Adirondacks than the wider 
valleys. The front will continue to push south early Monday, with 
models denoting it stalling out just south of our CWA from Lake 
Ontario into the Hudson Valley and curling to the Northeast towards 
Maine. Drier northern air will filter south into the area with a 
drying trend for Monday. Temperatures will also fall into the low to 
mid 70s with the cooler north air.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The weather pattern will feature channeled flow against 
a deep layer high in the southeastern US and a strong, compact upper 
low shifting slowly eastward across Canada. Systems with Pacific 
origins will get sucked into this fast flow bringing rounds of rain. 
Surface high pressure in far eastern Canada will try and keep warm, 
humid air from lifting northeastwards, and so we will be on the 
stable and dry side of things for the most part on Tuesday. We still 
should observe increased clouds and some rain along the southern 
portions of our forecast area. A stronger area of low pressure will 
develop over the Great Lakes region on Wednesday, and that should 
provide the focus for more active weather conditions. The interface 
of dry, stable conditions on the western periphery of departing high 
pressure and humid, modified tropical Pacific air will create the 
potential for showers and thunderstorms beginning late Wednesday 
afternoon. Elevated instability could allow thunderstorm activity to 
persist overnight before the system departs early Thursday morning. 
Synoptic scale models are starting to depict this feature as the one 
that produces most of our rainfall next week. Dynamically, the 
system appears quite vigorous and simulated IR satellite off the GFS 
is showing the potential for cool cloud tops associated with the 
elevated convection and strong isentropic lift. We'll continue to 
keep an eye on this feature.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Through 12Z Sunday...Only KSLK has some fog left at their
terminal, and this will soon lift. Clear skies are expected
the next several hours northwest to west winds in eastern
Vermont and southwest to south winds from the Green Mountains
westwards. Winds will trend more southerly over time, and may
become somewhat variable after sunset. About 03z-08z, LLWS will
be possible for several terminals with winds around 2000 ft agl
increasing to 30-40 knots out of the west ahead of an incoming
front. Steady winds will also remain overnight as clouds begin
to overspread the region. Some virga will be possible early
Sunday. Limited, if any, fog development is expected for later 
tonight.

Outlook...

Sunday: VFR. Scattered SHRA, Isolated TSRA.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Monday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Monday Night: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Tuesday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Tuesday Night: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Likely SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Wednesday: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. Likely SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.

&&

NY...None.
